newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore economists see more strife for exports.
newsitem.headline: Singapore economists see more strife for exports.

text.p: Singapore's manufacturers are still struggling to make headway amid slower regional growth and weak global electronics demand, economists said on Friday.
The first quarter's economic growth at 3.8 percent, down from 5.8 percent in the last quarter of 1996, was mostly dampened by the poor performance of the manufacturing sector.
The Ministry of Trade and Industry, announcing the first quarter figures on Friday, said it still forecast the economy would grow five to seven percent in 1997.
But economists told Reuters the second half of the year would have to be a lot better to achieve that.
"Manufacturing is still quite bad and electronics have not been performing well. Real signs for a turnaround are not there yet," said Wong Keng Siong, an economist at Yamaichi Securities.

The manufacturing sector shrank 6.7 percent, after contracting 0.7 percent in the previous quarter and by 3.9 percent in the third quarter of 1996. Manufacturing output for March registered a fall of 8.5 percent year-on-year.
Manufacturing accounts for about 23 percent of employment in Singapore. Electronics account for nearly 60 percent of Singapore's non-oil exports.
Economists had predicted the electronics slowdown was bottoming out and that orders should pick up during the second half of the year, in line with stronger global markets.
While signs of recovery were increasing, most still believed the immediate economic outlook remained cloudy.

Some said the lower 3.8 percent year-on-year in gross domestic product (GDP) growth could be blamed on a higher 11.5 percent base for first quarter 1996 and should even out in subsequent quarters, where the base of comparison is lower.
Others pinned optimism for a recovery in the second-half on improved growth in finance and business services, which posted surprising growth of 10.5 percent for the first quarter.

"An improvement in the manufacturing sectors with this robustness in the services sectors will result in higher GDP growth figures in the coming quarters," said Rajeev Malik, senior economist with Jardine Fleming.
He said investors were normally fixated on the manufacturing sector performance and tended to ignore developments in the services sector.
Market watchers had expected government curbs on the property market a year ago would hit financial services.
"Real estate is one of the main components of business services. That was one of the fears for the second-half of 1996," said Liew Yin Sze, economist with J.M Sassoon.
Another glimmer of hope for recovery in the mid-term was what economists viewed as measures to increase export and labour competitiveness.
The Singapore dollar, which until recently enjoyed a long and steady appreciation against the U.S. dollar, has fallen to about 1.43 from 1.39 in December.
"It's a cautious move by the government to ease costs at a critical time," Liew added.
He said the neutral to expansionary policy should ease business costs and the price of hiring foreign workers in labour-short Singapore.
